es.summary: Una identidad eliminó uno o más objetos Event de Kubernetes mediante la API. Puede ser una limpieza administrativa o un intento de borrar el rastro de actividad maliciosa en el clúster.
es.what_it_detects: Registros de auditoría de Kubernetes con verb igual a 'delete' sobre objectRef.resource igual a 'events'. No cubre el verbo 'deletecollection' ni la expiración automática de eventos por TTL.
es.why_it_matters: Los eventos de Kubernetes muestran la creación de pods, fallos de imagen, reinicios y cambios de programación. Borrarlos oculta actividad reciente del atacante: es eliminación de indicadores (ATT&CK T1070) y figura en el Threat Matrix for Kubernetes de Microsoft.
triage_steps: Identifique al actor: user.username, user.groups, sourceIPs y userAgent. Determine si es una persona, un service account o un controlador.
Revise objectRef.namespace y objectRef.name: qué eventos se borraron y a qué pods, nodos o despliegues se referían.
Confirme el resultado en responseStatus.code: un 200 indica borrado exitoso; un 403 indica un intento bloqueado por RBAC, igualmente relevante.
Mida el volumen: cuente los borrados de events del mismo usuario en +/- 15 minutos; borrados masivos o en varios namespaces son más sospechosos.
Pivote por el mismo usuario y sourceIPs en +/- 15 minutos: busque pods/exec, creación de pods privilegiados, lectura de secrets o cambios de rolebindings.
Si el actor es un service account, identifique el pod que usa ese token y valide si la herramienta legítimamente limpia eventos.
Recupere los eventos borrados desde un sink externo (SIEM, exportador de eventos) si existe, y revise alertas previas para el mismo usuario o namespace.
Consulte con el dueño del clúster si existe un ticket de cambio o mantenimiento que justifique la limpieza.
false_positives: Administradores que ejecutan kubectl delete events para limpiar ruido durante una depuración.
Operadores o herramientas de limpieza que borran eventos antiguos de forma programada.
Pipelines de CI/CD o pruebas que restablecen clústeres o namespaces efímeros.
response_steps: Verifique con el responsable de la identidad si la acción fue autorizada antes de tomar medidas.
Si no fue autorizada, preserve los logs de auditoría y los eventos exportados para la investigación.
Revoque o rote las credenciales, tokens o kubeconfig del actor y suspenda el service account comprometido.
Investigue y revierta los cambios que el atacante intentó ocultar: pods, workloads, rolebindings o secrets accedidos.
Restrinja en RBAC el permiso delete sobre events a las identidades que realmente lo necesitan y envíe los eventos a un almacenamiento externo.
es.severity_rationale: Severidad media: la acción tiene usos administrativos legítimos, pero borrar eventos indica posible evasión y amerita revisión del contexto.

en.summary: An identity deleted one or more Kubernetes Event objects through the API. This may be administrative cleanup or an attempt to erase traces of malicious activity in the cluster.
en.what_it_detects: Kubernetes audit records with verb equal to 'delete' on objectRef.resource equal to 'events'. It does not cover the 'deletecollection' verb or automatic TTL expiry of events.
en.why_it_matters: Kubernetes events record pod creation, image pull failures, restarts and scheduling changes. Deleting them hides recent attacker activity: indicator removal (ATT&CK T1070), listed in Microsoft's Threat Matrix for Kubernetes.
triage_steps: Identify the actor: user.username, user.groups, sourceIPs and userAgent. Decide whether it is a person, a service account or a controller.
Review objectRef.namespace and objectRef.name: which events were deleted and which pods, nodes or deployments they referenced.
Check responseStatus.code: 200 means the deletion succeeded; 403 means RBAC blocked an attempt, which is still relevant.
Measure volume: count event deletions by the same user within +/- 15 minutes; bulk or multi-namespace deletions are more suspicious.
Pivot on the same user and sourceIPs within +/- 15 minutes: look for pods/exec, privileged pod creation, secret reads or rolebinding changes.
If the actor is a service account, find the pod using that token and confirm whether the tool legitimately cleans up events.
Recover deleted events from an external sink (SIEM, event exporter) if available, and check earlier alerts for the same user or namespace.
Ask the cluster owner whether a change ticket or maintenance window justifies the cleanup.
false_positives: Administrators running kubectl delete events to clear noise while debugging.
Operators or cleanup tools that delete old events on a schedule.
CI/CD pipelines or tests that reset ephemeral clusters or namespaces.
response_steps: Confirm with the identity's owner whether the action was authorized before acting.
If unauthorized, preserve audit logs and exported events for the investigation.
Revoke or rotate the actor's credentials, tokens or kubeconfig and disable the compromised service account.
Investigate and roll back what the attacker tried to hide: pods, workloads, rolebindings or accessed secrets.
Restrict RBAC delete permission on events to identities that need it, and ship events to external storage.
en.severity_rationale: Medium fits because the action has legitimate admin uses, but deleting events suggests possible evasion and warrants a context review.

positive.description: An interactive user deletes an event in the payments namespace with kubectl from an external IP.
A service account deletes an event in kube-system shortly after a pod exec.

negative.description: A user lists events with kubectl get events; the verb is list, not delete.
A user deletes a pod; the verb is delete but the resource is pods, not events.
